desc:
You get three non-empty integer arrays a, b, c, each sorted in non-decreasing order. Choose one element from each array and let the spread of the choice be max - min of the three chosen values.

Return the smallest possible spread.

a = [1, 4, 10], b = [2, 15, 20], c = [10, 12]
choose 10, 15, 10 → spread 15 - 10 = 5
result = 5
constraints: Each array is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Trying all triples costs the product of the lengths. Use the sortedness: start with the three smallest elements.
In the current triple, the minimum element is the one that limits the spread. Which pointer should move to have any chance of improving?
Always advance the pointer that points at the current minimum (moving the others can only increase the maximum). Record max - min at every step and stop when one array is exhausted.
editorial: Keep one pointer per array, all starting at 0. At every step compute the spread of the three current values and update the best. Then advance the pointer whose value is the smallest of the three.

Why this is safe: let m be the current minimum, belonging to array X. Any triple that uses this element of X together with later elements of the other two arrays has a maximum at least as large as today's maximum, and the same minimum m (or smaller), so its spread is no better than today's. The element is therefore finished and can be skipped without losing the optimum.

Every step advances one pointer, so there are at most |a| + |b| + |c| steps: O(n) time, O(1) space. The same idea, extended to k arrays with a heap, gives the classic “smallest range covering elements from k lists” problem.
